notes.meaning: Jesus returns from the Jordan River filled with the Holy Spirit and is led by the Spirit into the lonely wilderness. He does not go there by his own whim, but under God's clear direction to prepare for his public work. Even when a person is close to God and walking in his Spirit, times of testing and struggle often follow.

For forty days, Jesus eats nothing and endures continuous attacks from the devil. God keeps him alive through this miraculous fast, but when the time ends, Jesus feels sharp human hunger. Israel failed and complained during forty years in the desert, but Jesus patiently obeys his Father.

The devil strikes right when Jesus is physically weak, challenging him to turn a stone into bread. Satan does not doubt that Jesus is God's Son, but tempts him to use his divine power selfishly instead of waiting on God. While the first man Adam fell by eating in a pleasant garden, Jesus stands firm in a harsh desert.

Jesus answers the devil by quoting Scripture from the book of Deuteronomy. He reminds Satan that physical bread is not the only thing keeping people alive, because human life depends entirely on God's sustaining word. Believers follow his example when they trust God's promises instead of taking wrong shortcuts to meet their needs.

The devil leads Jesus up high and shows him every kingdom of the inhabited world in a single second. This rapid vision puts all the wealth, power, and glory of human empires on display at once. Satan uses dazzling sights to tempt people to take their eyes off God.

The devil claims that all the kingdoms and their glory belong to him and that he can give them to anyone he chooses. While Satan holds a temporary, limited rule over a fallen world by God's permission, his claim to own everything is an arrogant lie. God alone rules the nations and decides who holds earthly power.

Satan offers to give all these kingdoms to Jesus on one condition: Jesus must bow down and worship him. The devil wants the Son of God to skip the suffering of the cross and gain the world by serving evil. This shows how Satan always tempts people to trade true worship of God for immediate power and comfort.

Jesus drives the temptation away with another command from Deuteronomy, stating that God alone must be worshiped and served. He makes it clear that no amount of worldly power is worth dishonoring the Lord. Believers must choose wholehearted loyalty to God above every earthly prize.

The devil brings Jesus to Jerusalem and sets him on the highest point of the temple wall. He dares Jesus to throw himself down, testing whether God will really protect him as his Son. Satan tries to push Jesus into showing off with a reckless public spectacle rather than following God's humble path.

Satan quotes from Psalm 91, claiming that God's angels will catch Jesus so he will not even hurt his foot on a stone. The devil twists this holy promise of divine care to tempt Jesus into taking a foolish, unnecessary risk. Misusing Bible verses to justify reckless behavior is a dangerous trap that believers must guard against.

Jesus counters the twisted scripture with a plain command from Deuteronomy: do not put the Lord your God to the test. True faith trusts God in times of trouble, but demanding that God prove his love by doing unnecessary miracles is proud and wrong. God wants his people to walk in quiet trust rather than trying to force his hand.

Having failed at every kind of attack, the devil leaves Jesus until a more favorable time arrives. Jesus wins a complete victory over the enemy by relying on God's truth. Even after winning a great battle against temptation, Christians must remain watchful, knowing that trials can return later.

Jesus returns to the district of Galilee strengthened and directed by the power of the Holy Spirit. He is now ready to begin his public work of teaching and performing miracles. News of his wisdom and mighty deeds spreads quickly across the surrounding towns.

Jesus teaches inside the local synagogues, the Jewish houses of study and prayer. The people are deeply impressed by his authority and speak highly of him everywhere he goes. God often grants a time of widespread favor and quiet before public ministry meets resistance.

Jesus travels to Nazareth, the town where he had grown up and lived for many years. On the Sabbath, he joins the community at the synagogue for public worship, just as he always did. He stands up to read the Scripture, setting an example for believers to faithfully gather for worship.

The synagogue attendant hands Jesus the scroll containing the book of the prophet Isaiah. Jesus deliberately unrolls the parchment until he finds the exact passage he wants to read. This selection was chosen on purpose to introduce his life's mission to his hometown.

Jesus reads Isaiah's prophecy declaring that God's Spirit is upon him to preach good news to the poor. God has sent him to announce freedom to prisoners, restore sight to the blind, and lift up those crushed by misery. These words describe how the Savior brings spiritual rescue and comfort to all who are broken by sin.

Jesus finishes the reading by proclaiming the year of the Lord's favor. This refers to the Old Testament Jubilee, a special celebration every fifty years when debts were erased and slaves were set free. Jesus stopped reading before the mention of God's judgment day, highlighting that his first coming brings God's mercy and forgiveness.

Jesus rolls up the parchment, gives it back to the attendant, and takes a seat. In Jewish worship, teachers sat down to explain the passage they had just read standing up. The whole congregation gazes at him with intense focus, waiting eagerly to hear his explanation.

Jesus begins his sermon with a stunning announcement: this ancient prophecy is being fulfilled right in front of them today. He is openly declaring that he himself is the promised Messiah sent by God to bring salvation. Hearing God's word calls every listener to recognize Jesus as the true Savior and trust him.

The listeners are amazed by the gracious and compelling way Jesus speaks. Yet they quickly stumble over their old memories, asking whether this is merely Joseph the carpenter's son. Because they were so familiar with his childhood, they struggle to believe that someone from their own neighborhood could be the Christ.
